en: *Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle One.

"Vajra" refers to that which is the most refined and solid among gold. It is produced from within gold; though refined a hundred times, it does not diminish. Its substance is extremely hard and sharp;
it cannot be broken by other things, yet there is nothing it cannot break. For example, prajñā can illuminate and shatter all [delusions].
It gives rise to greed, anger, ignorance, craving, and all inverted views. *Prajñā* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "wisdom.
Its essential nature is empty and harmonious, and its illuminating function is sovereign and free; therefore, it is called *prajñā*. *Pāramitā* is also a Sanskrit term.
In the language of China, this is called "reaching the other shore. To wish to reach the other shore, one must rely upon *prajñā*.
This shore refers to the place where sentient beings commit misdeeds and suffer, falling into a state of sinking and delusion.

The other shore refers to the ultimate realm of all Buddhas, where human desires are completely purified and all is luminous, upright, and majestic. *Jing* means a path; it is like a route or track. That is to say, if one wishes—
To reach the other shore, one must necessarily follow this path. There are six *pāramitās*: first, generosity (*dāna*), which crosses over stinginess and greed;

second, ethical discipline (*śīla*), which crosses over lust and depravity; third, patience (*kṣānti*), which crosses over anger and resentment; fourth, diligence (*vīrya*), which crosses over indolence and regression;
fifth, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which crosses over distraction; and sixth, wisdom (*prajñā*), which crosses over ignorance and delusion. Each occupies one of these six perfections.
Only prajñā can give rise to the eighty-four thousand types of wisdom; thus, it encompasses the six perfections and prepares all myriad practices.

Regarding the Buddha’s words in the Sanskrit language, none in the Middle Kingdom understood their meaning. In the third year of Hongshi, Yao Qin welcomed Kumārajīva to Chang’an and treated him with the etiquette due to a National Teacher.
He requested that Kumārajīva use the language of the Middle Kingdom [to explain them].
This sutra has been translated to instruct future students. The true nature of humanity is inherently void, lucid, and unclouded;
it exists eternally throughout the kalpas. Alas, it is obscured by myriad desires, causing one to sink into the sea of suffering and undergo endless retribution.
Out of his great compassion, our Buddha specifically preached this sutra, like using a raft to cross a ford and reach the other shore.
That which is called "vajra" (diamond/thunderbolt) refers to the fact that no phenomenon can escape the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*).
Among these five elements, gold alone is the most firm, sharp, and enduring. Wood eventually decays; water eventually dries up;
fire eventually extinguishes; and earth eventually collapses. When gold is applied to wood, it can be fashioned into functional implements.
When immersed in water, its radiance remains deep and ever-renewed; when cast into fire, it becomes more refined through a hundred smeltings;
when buried in the earth, it remains indestructible for eternal kalpas. Its position lies in the northwest, where it can crush and break all things.
If a person can apply it to their own body, they may sever the demonic influences within themselves and eliminate the malevolent spirits across ten thousand li.

The Confucian possesses the precious sword Longquan (Dragon Spring) to bring peace to the state and stabilize the nation; the Daoist possesses the precious sword Green Snake to sever and eliminate worldly desires;
the Buddha possesses the precious vajra pestle to subdue the Māras. In the Great Changes (*Dàyì*), Qian is the primary hexagram;
in the Primordial Gate (*Yuánmén*), the Golden Elixir (*Jīndān*) is the primary practice; this sutra takes the Vajra as its primary focus. One who attains this Prajñā realizes the Western [Paradise].
The Land of Immeasurable Life is the Western Golden Quarter. How great indeed is the significance of gold!
Therefore, the diamond (*vajra*) is used as a metaphor. *Prajñā* means wisdom. In the daily lives of human beings, people strive for fame and greed for profit.
A hundred forms of deceit and hypocrisy emerge; even at the moment of death, the mind remains unsatisfied.
One considers oneself clever and quick-witted, unaware that one is drowning in the bitter sea of sin and affliction—this is true folly. One must certainly employ wisdom to shatter this delusion.
Solely upholding the firm and vigorous will, with courageous and diligent progress, and clearly realizing one’s own nature—how could one not reach that shore of the Way?
Would one not be identical to the Buddhas in their pure and equal bodies? In sum, this is the Vajra-like Samādhi, the Prajñā Dharma, and the realization of the fruit of the Pāramitās.
This commentary was annotated by Master Shigong Tianji regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
The meaning of the character "bo" (波) is already very clear in its interpretation; therefore, I have preserved the original explanation.
This was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty under imperial decree.
During the era of the Yao Qin translations, the Later Qin Yao clan established their capital at Chang’an to distinguish themselves from the Fu clan of the Former Qin.
Therefore, it is called "Yao Qin. Kumārajīva is the name of the translator of the scriptures. Jīva’s father was named Kumārayaśas and his mother was named Jīvā.
Their ancestors resided in India, and for generations their family had served as prime ministers. His father was renowned for his intelligence;
he abdicated his position to leave the household life and traveled to study in Kucha. When the King of Kucha heard of him, he compelled his daughter to become his wife.
...he was born as Kumārajīva. From the day Kumārajīva was in the womb, his mother’s wisdom and eloquence increased, much like when Śāriputra was in his mother’s womb.

Once Kumārajīva was born, his mother immediately began studying Buddhism and practicing the path, attaining the realization of the first fruit (srotāpanna). From the age of seven, he also studied the Buddha-vehicle together with her;
receiving sūtras from a teacher, he could recite a thousand verses daily. At nine years of age, he accompanied his mother to Kaśmīra, where he relied upon—
There was a renowned and virtuous Dharma Master named Bandhudatta who studied the sūtras and śāstras of the Hīnayāna.
At the age of twelve, his mother took him back to the kingdom of Yuezhi. On the northern mountains there, an arhat beheld him and marveled at him, saying to his mother:
"You must guard this boy well. If, upon reaching thirty-five years of age, he does not violate the precepts, he shall save people in a manner no less than that of Kātyāyanīputra."
If he were one who had broken the precepts, he would be merely a Dharma Master of superficial brilliance and refined arts.

He then proceeded to the country of Śākala, where he beheld the Buddha’s bowl and placed it upon his head. Suddenly, he felt the bowl was heavy and could no longer support its weight; he cried out involuntarily and set it down.
His mother asked him the reason for this, and he answered her with the principle of "mind-only. He then returned to Kucha, where his fame eclipsed that of all other countries.
Regarding the four *vidyāsthānas*, the five *vibhāṣā* treatises, and various arts such as Yin-Yang, astrology, and mathematics, there was nothing whose subtleties and profundities he did not master.
He followed Vimalākṣa to study the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* from a scholastic perspective, and he also studied under Sūryasoma.

Consulting with and receiving instruction from the Mahāyāna, he finally realized the error of his previous study of the Hīnayāna. Thus, he devoted himself exclusively to practicing the Mahāyāna and extensively sought its essential meanings.
After some time, Kumārajīva’s mother, having foreseen the impending decline of the Kucha kingdom, took leave to travel to India.

Having advanced to the realization of the third fruit (srotāpanna), she said to Kumārajīva as she was about to depart: "The profound teachings of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) shall be propagated in the capital of Qin; however, for yourself—"
"How could it be that my body is now in such a disadvantageous state? Kumārajīva replied, "The practice of a Bodhisattva is to benefit others even at the cost of one's own life.
If this great transformation can indeed be carried out, I would have no regrets even if I were cast into a cauldron of fire. He then remained in Kucha, residing at the King’s New Temple.
Later, he traveled again to Kaśmīra. For his teacher Bandhudatta, he fully expounded the sublime meanings of the Mahāyāna.

Bandhudatta was moved to realization and, in turn, paid homage to Kumārajīva, taking him as his Mahāyāna master. From this time on, the Way spread throughout the Western Regions (Sīnyatra), and its fame flowed to the Eastern Continent (Jambudvīpa).
It was during the ninth year of the Jianyuan era of Fu Jian of Former Qin that a strange star appeared in the Western Regions.
The Bureau of Astronomy reported: "A man of great virtue and wisdom shall enter to assist the Central Kingdom. Yao Xian said:
"I have heard that there is Kumārajīva in Kucha and Dao’an in Xiangyang; could it not be these two men?
Thereupon, he first sent for Dao’an, and subsequently dispatched General of the Light Cavalry Lü Guang to lead seventy thousand troops to invade Kucha and bring [Kumārajīva] back.

When Kumārajīva arrived in Western Liang, Guṇabhadra heard that Fu Jian had been assassinated by Yao Chang. He then took control of the territory of Liang and ascended the throne as the King of the Three Rivers;
Kumārajīva likewise remained there. When Yao Chang ascended the throne, he too heard of the Master’s reputation and invited him repeatedly, but Guṇabhadra did not consent.

Upon Yao Chang’s death, his son Yao Xing was established. Yao Xing again invited him, but [Guṇabhadra] did not consent. Guṇabhadra died, and his son Yao Long was established. Yao Xing then launched a military expedition against Liang.
He invited Kumārajīva, who arrived in Chang’an and was honored with the etiquette due to a National Teacher. This was during the third year of the Hongshi era.
Upon examining the previously translated sūtras and śāstras, he found that they mostly did not correspond to the Sanskrit originals.
Consequently, he assembled more than eight hundred śramaṇas and translated ninety-eight works, totaling three hundred and ninety volumes. These were the texts he translated.

This sutra is titled the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. As Kumārajīva was approaching death, he gathered his assembly and said, "I have been presumptuous in my ignorance, falsely assuming the role of a translator.
If what I have transmitted is free from error, may my tongue remain uncorrupted after my body has been consumed by fire. Later, it was indeed so.
Thus we know that the Master’s tongue manifested the Tathāgata’s mark of the broad and long tongue; they were equal and without distinction.

There are differences. Thus, although this sutra has been translated six times, those who have followed it as their primary authority have all relied upon the Qin version; the present commentary follows this one.
The Buddha was born in the western land of Jambudvīpa on the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Jiayin, the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty in the eastern land.
He entered through the right side of his mother, Māyā. Immediately—
He emerged from the right side [of his mother’s womb]. He entered *nirvāṇa* on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu’s reign, the year of *Renshen*.
One thousand and seventeen years later, in the tenth year of the Yongping era of the Later Han, the year of *Wucheng*, his teaching first began to spread throughout China.
"Buddha" (*Fó*) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit sound; in the language of China, it means "Awakened" (*jué*). This refers to one who, regarding all things...

Among sentient beings, he is one who is capable of awakening. Internally, he awakens to the absence of all deluded thoughts; externally, he awakens to being unstained by the six sense objects. It is also said that he is the Teacher.
Being without form yet possessing form, he is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. Being form yet not form, he is the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha.
Being neither form nor non-form, he is the Dharmakāya Buddha. Śākyamuni Buddha expounded the Prajñāpāramitā twice.
The twelve-year compilation comprises more than six hundred fascicles. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is the five hundred and seventy-seventh fascicle;

it is titled the "Chapter on Severing Doubt" (*Cchidrasaṃśaya-parivarta*) and constitutes the essential summary of the entire *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. For this reason, it alone has been widely circulated.
It enables those who maintain and recite it to attain firm resolve and give rise to wisdom. One need only value constant and uninterrupted recitation, and a natural resonance will surely follow.

The benefits thereof are inexhaustible. This sutra has been printed in the greatest number of editions throughout ancient and modern times; consequently, errors and corruptions have frequently occurred.

Although Master Lianchi collated and corrected it, mis-transmissions still persist across various versions. In this edition, the original text has been meticulously examined and verified, with every character rendered with absolute precision.
Furthermore, punctuation marks have been added beneath the phrases, and the text is divided into three categories. Those spoken by the Buddha are marked with...
The circle (○) used here for what was spoken by Subhūti; the double circle (◎) used for what was compiled by Ānanda;
and the dot (·) used for [the rest]—these are provided so that readers may grasp the meaning of the sutra at a glance, and its intent shall become self-evident.
Written reverently by the Dharma-wheel śramaṇa Xingmin, seventy-first-generation descendant of the Buddha.

Regarding this commentary on the sutra that I have authored: having observed that there are many commentaries by various schools, I examined them all with great care and found none that included marginal annotations (*pangzhu*).
Fearing that readers might fail to achieve realization, or that those who had realized it might be unable to recite it, I have thus provided detailed and clear marginal annotations.
This allows the reader to grasp the meaning at a glance and to contemplate it at any time, thereby understanding its principles and practicing all signless and unconditioned dharmas.
This is not merely to teach people the vain recitation [of mantras] to obtain superior merit;
rather, it concerns the field of blessings cultivated internally. That which is cultivated externally and is seen and heard by all is called "yangde" (manifest virtue). Internally...
To cultivate that which people neither see nor hear is called "hidden virtue" (*yin de*). Virtue with form and conditioned activity does not equal the merit of the formless and unconditioned.
Cultivation externally does not equal the merit of internal cultivation. Virtuous deeds manifest in the world (*yang de*) do not equal the greatness of hidden virtue.
This is because one perceives the dharma of non-form in *prajñā*; thus, all six perfections and myriad practices should be realized within this essence.
This signless Dharma is to be cultivated; therefore, one should successively teach others to receive, uphold, read, and recite it, explaining it for others so that they may know this signless Dharma.
It is subtle and profound, capable of being cultivated and realized by oneself, leading to the illumination of the mind and the seeing of its nature.
Indeed, those who believe and accept it must first understand the general outline of the Tripitaka and eliminate the six sense faculties.

After the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), one must further eliminate the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) until they are entirely empty; only then can one enter the four marks of non-self, non-person, and so forth.
When these four marks of non-self, non-person, and so forth are naturally realized, one’s mind becomes supple and resilient, and one embraces all things with compassion.

Thus, the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) and six sense objects do not adhere through defilement, and one perceives no person who could bring humiliation upon oneself. One will then naturally exert diligence in the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Never regressing, the four great elements do not exist; the five aggregates are entirely empty. As mind and mind redeem one another, they are naturally pure;
thus, self-nature is eternally empty and free from obstruction. The single truth is revealed, its light pervading everywhere.
There is nothing it does not illuminate. The sūtras spoken by the Buddha constitute the Piṭakas;
none of them fail to elucidate the meaning of the four propositions. The Buddha-dharma is thus encompassed without exception.

Therefore, the dharmas of the four marks—such as self and person—are not merely the marrow of the *Vajracchedikā* alone, but are truly the marrow of the entire Tripiṭaka. Those who read the sūtras should understand these four.
This work constitutes the complete essence of the sutra; it may truly be said to be one that accords with the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtras.
If those who revere the Buddha can follow this in practice, what concern need they have about not reaching the other shore?
This is my aspiration. Thus ends the preface.

Section One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly. From "Thus have I heard" up to "arranged his seat and sat down," this section serves as the introduction to the time and place where the assembly gathered for the preaching of the Dharma;
therefore, it is titled "The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly."
Thus have I heard. "Thus" (evam) means "in this way. "I" (aham) refers to the compiler of the sutra himself.
The Venerable Ānanda said: "In this manner, I personally heard this Dharma from the Buddha."
"At one time. "At one time" refers to the time when the Prajñā was being taught.
"Buddha. "Buddha" means awakening. Because he has awakened himself and awakened others, and because his practice of awakening is perfected, he is named Buddha.
This refers to Śākyamuni Buddha.
"Is present. "Is present" means wherever [he] is located. Śrāvastī.
Śrāvastī is the country where King Prasenajit resides. Jeta’s Grove.
"Jeta's" refers to the name of King Prasenajit's crown prince; it is the grove of trees within Jeta Park, belonging to Jeta.
Because it was planted [by Jeta], it is called "Jeta’s Grove.
As for "Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park": in the kingdom of Śrāvastī there was an elder who was a minister to the king;
his original name was Sudatta, but because he always delighted in giving alms to the orphaned and destitute, he was named Anāthapiṇḍada ("Feeder of the Destitute").
The Elder, Anāthapiṇḍika, built a vihāra in the Jeta Grove and invited the Buddha to preach the Dharma;
therefore, it is called "Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s [Park]."
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. In Sanskrit, *bhikṣu* means "one who begs" (*qǐshì*) in the language of China.
This refers to those who, above, beg for the Dharma from the Buddha to clarify their own true nature, and below, beg for food from others to enable worldly people to plant seeds of merit.

Since the Buddha was about to expound the wondrous principle of emptiness and formlessness, it was necessary that only those who had attained the profound path could comprehend it; how could it be otherwise?
How could they be matched by ordinary bhikṣus? These bhikṣus belong to the class of bodhisattvas and arhats.
They were present in a company of one thousand two hundred and fifty; indeed, they were in a company of one thousand two hundred and fifty.
All these disciples constantly attended upon and dwelt together with the Buddha wherever he preached the Dharma.
"At that time" means at that particular time. "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān):
because the Buddha is the most honored one within the three realms, he is called the World-Honored One. The "three realms" are the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
"At mealtime. At mealtime" means when it is about to be time for the morning meal.
"Donning the robes" means donning the robe of gentleness and patience; that is, the saṃghāṭī.
Holding the bowl. Holding the bowl. Holding the bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings, he entered the great city of Śrāvastī.
He entered the great city of Śrāvastī. Since the garden was outside the city walls of the kingdom of Śrāvastī, it is said that he "entered."
He went for alms within that city. He went for alms within that city. The Buddha was the crown prince of a Golden Wheel-turning King;

who would not have made offerings to him? Yet he personally carried his bowl to beg for food, desiring to teach sentient beings to abandon arrogance and eliminate this greedy mind, and wishing to ensure that monks of future generations would not accumulate wealth and treasures. Thus...
Refining one's spiritual nature is like a true gentleman who plans for the Way and not for food.
Having completed his alms-round in sequence, he proceeds in order; he does not bypass the poor to follow the wealthy, nor does he abandon the lowly to seek the noble.
The Tathāgata’s great compassion is impartial and makes no distinctions; he simply goes to every place in due order.
"Returning to his original location" means returning to the Jeta Grove after having finished begging for alms.
"Having finished eating" means that the meal has been completed.
Having gathered his robes and bowl and washed his feet— meaning he had put away his *kāṣāya* and almsbowl and cleansed his feet—
he did so to purify his physical actions as he was about to enter the place for meditation. Thus,
he gathered up his robes and bowl so that his mind would be free from attachment, and he washed his feet to cleanse his body.
He spread out his seat and sat down. Then he spread out his seat and sat down. "Spreading" (*fu*) means to arrange; it refers to arranging the seats in their proper order and then sitting.

This coming and going, moving and stillness of our Buddha—spontaneously in accord with the Way—is something I have personally witnessed clearly and recorded in its entirety. It was from such circumstances that this Dharma assembly arose.
Section Two: The Chapter on Subhūti’s Request. It is called the "Chapter on Subhūti’s Request" because Subhūti rose from his seat to question the Buddha.
Regarding the term "time":
it refers to the time when the Buddha had returned to the park from entering the city and was seated upon the prepared throne.
"Elder" (sthavira) refers to one who is venerable by virtue of their merit. Among the assembly of disciples, he alone is addressed as "Elder" because of his supreme merit.
"Subhūti" is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the language of China, it means "One Who Understands Emptiness. He is also named "Suxian" (Śubhavyūha), which signifies that he is able to...
He understood and realized the principle of emptiness and was skilled at manifesting it.
"In the midst of the great assembly" refers to being among the assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
He rose from his seat. Subhūti immediately rose from his own seat, adjusted his demeanor, and stood up from his place.
He bared his right shoulder; by baring his right shoulder, he showed that he did not dare to treat his teacher with disrespect. To the east...

In the lands of the East, one bares the shoulder because of the practice of expressing regret and seeking absolution; in the Western lands, one bares the shoulder because of the custom of performing respectful salutations.
One places the right knee upon the ground. Placing the right knee upon the ground is to demonstrate that one does not dare to turn left from the Way.

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The right is the Right Path; the left is the Deviant Path. Thus, one must place the right knee upon the ground. The baring of the shoulder is likewise [for this purpose].
Baring the right shoulder signifies the intention to eliminate evil through rectitude; it demonstrates the sincerity of one’s physical karma (*kāyakarman*).
Joining the palms (*añjali*) means that the mind merges with the Way and the Way merges with the mind, thereby manifesting one’s taking of refuge.
"Reverence. As for reverence, it means to manifest a solemn mind and respectful intent, thereby demonstrating the sincerity of one's mental karma (*manas-karman*).
Thus he addressed the Buddha, having first manifested inner and outer sincerity before speaking to the Buddha. "To address" (*bāi*) means to initiate; "to speak" (*yán*) means to utter.

"Speech" refers to praise. "Rare, World-Honored One! "Rare" means few; it is like saying, "World-Honored One, there are few such as you. "Tathāgata": "Tathāgata" is a general title for a Buddha. "As" (tathā) means not arising; "come" (āgata) means not ceasing. Alternatively: ... [text continues] ...This is the meaning of "Tathāgata. Furthermore, "Tathāgata" is a term that encompasses all Buddhas. It is said that because they have realized the *dharmatā* (the nature of reality) exactly as it is, they are called "Tathāgatas. Moreover, the term "Tathāgata" is used to indicate that they have attained the ultimate fruit of the path. Furthermore, it is said that because they have come from the realm of *tathatā* (suchness), they are called "Tathāgatas. Also, it is said that because they have gone to the realm of *tathatā*, they are called "Tathāgatas. Furthermore, it is said that because they have realized the *dharmatā* exactly as it is, they are called "Tathāgatas. Moreover, it is said that because they have manifested the supreme enlightenment, they are called "Tathāgatas. Furthermore, it is said that because they have transcended birth and death, they are called "Tathāgatas. Also, it is said that because they have entered *nirvāṇa*, they are called "Tathāgatas. Moreover, it is said that because they have severed all fetters (*saṃyojana*), they are called "Tathāgatas. Also, it is said that because they have realized the stable (*sthira*), they are called "Tathāgatas. Moreover, it is said that because they have realized the constant (*nitya*), they are called "Tathāgatas. Also, it is said that because they have realized the eternal (*śāśvata*), they are called "Tathāgatas. It is cut off. One should not seek it through form or color.

Profound stillness and eternal quiescence is the fundamental mind of all Buddhas;
this is what is called the thirty-two marks. This is called the thirty-two marks. The thirty-two marks are like the categories of eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and so forth;
these are the Buddha of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). All that possesses marks is entirely illusory and false.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Buddha, having heard that Subhūti had attained a thorough and penetrating realization of the dharma of the emptiness of the nature of *prajñā*, again addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Among all things valued in the world, none surpasses one's own body and life. He then instructed him with this recitation:
The Sūtra’s merit states: "That which I call the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is the wisdom of *prajñā*.

Regarding the wondrous thirty-two marks of the Buddha’s body, through the power of *prajñā*, one clearly perceives them as illusory and not real.
If one can reverently accept, uphold, and maintain this [wisdom], one will truly be able to awaken to the illusory and clarify the real.
With a mind that is ultimately real and free from delusion, there is nowhere one goes that is not good, and nowhere one goes that is not merit. All the merit and virtue thus obtained—

Chapter Fourteen: The Section on the Quiescence of the Signless. This is the section on the natural quiescence that is free from all forms and signs.
At that time—“at that time” meaning at that particular moment—Subhūti heard the words of the Buddha.
"Upon hearing this sutra spoken"—that is, upon hearing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*—he "deeply understood its meaning and intent.
"Deeply understanding" means attaining great enlightenment within the mind. "Meaning and intent" refers to the principles and underlying purpose.
As for the "wisdom eye," the heart of a sage possesses seven apertures; with a single hearing, he attains a thousand awakenings. This is the eye of wisdom.

Thus, he deeply understood the Buddha’s teaching. Employing the *prajñā* of the self-nature of true emptiness—which is as firm and sharp as a vajra—he was able to sever all afflictions of various marks (*nimitta*).
Through his realization of the meaning and intent of the true reality of the *prajñā* of the emptiness of nature, he was moved by such extreme joy that grief arose;

Being unable to believe, understand, accept, or uphold [the teaching], they have brought shame upon the wondrous Dharma transmitted from my Buddha-heart.
Weeping with tears of sorrow, they suddenly became unaware of their own weeping; what flows from the nose is called *tai* (mucus), and what flows from the eyes is called *lei* (tears).
Great pain is called *bei* (sorrow); slight pain is called *qi* (weeping). This means that first there are tears, followed by great pain, and subsequently slight pain.
"Slight pain" refers to the point where the pain is being withdrawn as it is about to be expressed.

When Subhūti heard the Dharma of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, he attained a profound understanding of its meaning and purpose, penetrating it thoroughly and clearly. Overcome with extreme joy, he was moved to sorrow; unconsciously, his tears flowed and he wept in grief.
He wept. First, he grieved that he had heard the Dharma so late; second, he grieved for those of the present and future, fearing they would be unable to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it.
Then he addressed the Buddha, speaking thus to the Buddha.
"Rare, World-Honored One!"—this is a word of praise. "Rare" means few. In this world, there are few such as our World-Honored One, who speaks such profound sutras.
The Buddha speaks thus because he relies upon the *prajñāpāramitā* that is originally empty, signless, and without characteristics.
If one enters the Prajñā of the true mark of ultimate emptiness— such a most wondrous and profound scripture—
then from the time I first began my cultivation and realization until now, I have by nature known how to maintain the six sense faculties so as not to enter the realms of the six sense objects. Thus,
I have gradually awakened to the principle of formlessness and have gradually detached myself from the realm of desire.
Gradually, both object and cognition vanish. Reflecting from the present back to the past, I realize how much was wasted in upholding the precepts and practicing cultivation;
only after such arduous discipline and asceticism have I finally attained the first stage of the Arhat path, which is free from desire.
The eye of wisdom that has been attained—possessing this eye of wisdom, one is well able to listen and awaken.

Having never before heard such a sutra, and having never before heard it, one immediately uses the *prajñā* of self-nature, which is empty and signless, to illuminate and shatter the falsity of all signs; thus, one immediately attains the vision of the self-nature of emptiness.
This is indeed the mutual manifestation that leads one to the shore of the Buddhas' perfection of awakening; such is this sutra.
I am now fortunate to have entered this Dharma assembly and have already heard this sutra, deeply understanding its profound meaning.
"Bhagavān, [the interlocutor] addressed the Bhagavān,
saying: 'If there should be another person, or yet another person,
who hears this sutra— that is, hears the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.'"
The mind of faith is pure. One believes in the purity of the prajñā of one's own mind.
By not abiding in any marks, the true mark arises; that is, the true mark of the emptiness and formlessness of prajñā arises.
"You should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit;
they accomplish the mind of the path to unsurpassed bodhi, which is the foremost and most rare merit. The Sixth Patriarch said: "All arise from within the pure essence."
The Prajñāpāramitā flows forth.
World-Honored One, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This true mark is the true mark of Prajñā."
This is precisely the signless (*animitta*). Emptiness is like the Great Spirit; it has no form or trace. It is the non-sign of the total emptiness of its own essence.
For this reason, the Tathāgata calls it the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If there were truly a mark, it would belong to that which is subject to destruction; it would be an insubstantial dharma.
Because it is a mark through the absence of marks, it exists eternally from antiquity and remains undestroyed for ten thousand kalpas. For this reason, the Tathāgata—
This is what is called the true nature of reality.
World-Honored One, [the disciple] addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Now that I have heard such a sutra as this, and now that I have personally received your instruction, my mind listens and my spirit attains realization."
To have faith, resolve, and uphold [this teaching]—to be able to give rise to the mind that has faith, resolves, and upholds it—is not difficult; therefore, it is not difficult.
However, if it were in a future age, during the final five hundred years, a time long after [the Buddha's passing].
Should there be sentient beings who hear this sutra, they will not go beyond its words;
they will recite it from memory, believe in it, understand it, and accept and uphold it. To have faith is already difficult, and to attain understanding and realization is even more so.
How much more so to be able to receive it into one's heart and maintain it without loss? Unless one possesses manifold roots of goodness, this is certainly impossible.
Such a person is indeed the most rare and extraordinary. This is because such a person’s roots of goodness do not stem from only one or two lifetimes;
it must have been through planting various roots of goodness over many successive lives that they have become able to be thus.
They are therefore the most rare and extraordinary of persons, difficult to encounter.
Why is this? Why is this? Such a person is rare indeed.
This person is without the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span.
In an age of turbid kalpas, such a person alone is able to believe, understand, accept, and uphold the absence of these four marks—self, person, and so forth.
Why is this so? Furthermore, if one further investigates why it is thus:
the mark of self—by means of which a person realizes the mark of self—is itself a non-mark;
it is fundamentally not a truly real or solid entity, and is therefore a non-mark.
The mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span— having realized that these marks of a person, a sentient being,
and a life-span are all illusory in nature and ultimately subject to decay.
This is precisely the absence of marks; it is precisely the absence of the four marks.
Why is this? To further inquire and explain why: it is because this constitutes the foremost rarity.
For such a person has already abandoned the attachment to the four marks. Since the four marks are absent, they do not perceive any cause that can be cultivated, nor any fruit.
This can be attained by departing from all marks (*sarva-nimitta*). This departure from all marks means that both self and dharmas are empty; the mind is perpetually serene and quiescent.
This is precisely the true characteristic of the emptiness of *prajñā*. It is the arrival at the shore of awakening of the *pāramitā*, and with all...
The Buddhas are indeed yoked together and drive side by side;
they are thus called the Buddhas, they are thus called the Buddhas.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: Having heard the Dharma of Prajñā as understood by Subhūti, [the Buddha] transcended all...
All marks are themselves called the Buddhas; because they profoundly accord with the principle of Prajñā, [the Buddha] addressed Subhūti, saying:
"So it is, so it is. "So it is" means that what has been said accords with this principle.
Furthermore, if there should be a person— whether of the present or the future—
who hears this sutra and hears this sublime Dharma of Prajñā, the Buddha says that such a person...
He is not startled; being without surprise, he is free from doubt. To be startled in heart is to be shocked by the excessiveness of his words.
He is not terrified; being without suspicion or fear, he is without dread. To be terrified in heart is to fear the loftiness of his Way.
He is not afraid. He does not fear avoidance and has no retreat. One who fears in their heart is timid regarding the difficulty of the practice.
You should know that such a person is extremely rare; you should know that such a person is extremely rare because they have departed from all marks, which is itself most rare.
Why is this? For what reason? It is because this person is truly rare. Indeed, this person’s seeds of wholesome roots are profound;
they have already attained a silent realization of the signless Dharma of Prajñā. There is no time when they do not practice Prajñā, and there is no time when they are not Prajñā.
Among the six perfections and the myriad practices, there is nothing that is not Prajñā. Therefore, they are able to hear this sutra. From themselves—
One who is able to believe, understand, accept, and uphold [this]—realizing that there is nothing therein to be startled by, nothing to be terrified of, and nothing to be feared—is truly rare indeed.
Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "You must know that the dharma of prajñā is signless (animitta). In summary:
The Buddha-dharma encompasses the six perfections and the myriad practices;
all Buddhas realize their *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without departing from this very principle of non-characteristic (*animitta*) Prajñā.

The Tathāgata speaks of the foremost *pāramitā*. What I have called the foremost *pāramitā* is indeed emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and the self-realization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this is what the Tathāgata calls the foremost *pāramitā*.

Furthermore, it is by means of giving (*dāna*) that one reaches the further shore of all Buddhas. The Buddha taught that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty of essence; within, nothing is perceived.
In giving, one does not perceive the mark of a self; externally, one does not perceive the mark of the person receiving the gift;
internally, one does not perceive the mark of the object being given; nor does one perceive the mark of the dharma of the foremost pāramitā.
It is not the foremost *pāramitā*. In giving, there is nothing given; there is no shore reached.
It is not the foremost *pāramitā*;
it is merely named the foremost *pāramitā*. It does nothing more than provisionally use this to awaken the deluded masses. Because it is non-existent...
By practicing giving without signs (*animitta*), one attains the further shore; this is called the first *pāramitā*.
Subhūti, the *pāramitā* of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is likewise so: it is patience without signs.
Through the *pāramitā* of patience, by means of patience, one does not give rise to a mind of anger; through the true nature (*dharmatā*), one reaches the state of all Buddhas.
It is the other shore.
The Tathāgata says it is not the perfection of patience; it is simply that true emptiness is originally without marks.
Internally, the Tathāgata does not perceive the mark of a self who practices patience; externally, he does not perceive the mark of a person who insults him; in between, he does not perceive a self.
The mark of being able to endure within the mind is such that one does not perceive even the dharma-mark of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
There is nothing to be endured, and there is nothing to be insulted. There is no shore to be reached. The Tathāgata says that this is precisely not the perfection of patience.
This is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Because one attains the further shore by means of patience that is without marks (*animitta*), it is called the perfection of patience;
it is also precisely the markless dharma of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Why is this? Why is this? The Tathāgata says that what is called the perfection of patience is not actually the perfection of patience;
it is merely designated as the perfection of patience.
Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:
As I recall in the past when King Kali cut and mangled my body,
you may observe that at that time I had no perception of a self. At that time, my mind was like empty space, and I did not give rise to the four marks.
Therefore, there is no mark of a self that undergoes dismemberment;
no mark of a person; no mark of a person who performs the dismemberment;
no mark of a sentient being; and no mark of a sentient being who fears dismemberment.
There is no mark of a self, nor any mark of a self that protects its life.
Why is this? Why is this? Because in the past, I severed my hands, feet, ears, and nose.
When the body is dismembered limb by limb—at the very moment it is being severed joint by joint—it may be said that this is the ultimate humiliation.
Yet, if there were any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; if there were these four notions—
One ought to give rise to resentment; one ought to give rise to a mind of hatred. How could I still wish that King Kali be delivered first by having his limbs cut off?
Not only in my recent life, but throughout this Bhadrakalpa, I have been able to remain free from these four signs.
Subhūti. The Buddha called out to Subhūti again.
He further recollected his past lives over five hundred eons; he reflected once more upon how, in the past, during those five hundred eons...
During the Auspicious Eon (*Bhadrakalpa*), he was a rishi of forbearance.
While acting as a rishi of forbearance, throughout those lifetimes, he had practiced the conduct of forbearance; even in past ages, there was no realm of the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
There is no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span. One is also able to be without these four marks of self, person, and so forth.

In recent times during the Bhadrakalpa, as well as when I recall back through five hundred lifetimes in the previous Kalpa of Adornment, I was entirely without these four marks; therefore, I have now attained the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should remain detached from all marks.
One who wishes to attain the Buddha-way must empty their mind and resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, remaining free from all traces of form; only then may they proceed.
By generating this mind for unsurpassed bodhi, one is able to abide [in it].
One should not generate the mind by abiding in form; one should not dwell with attachment on the marks of form, nor give rise to thoughts of it being desirable.
One should not dwell on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena when generating the mind;
one should not abide in attachment to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor give rise to thoughts of desire.
One should generate a mind that dwells nowhere; one should generate that mind within the state of non-abiding. Thus, this mind—
Perfectly penetrating and unimpeded; truly pure and free from desire; not bound by any signs whatsoever—one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere amidst the signs of the six sense objects.
Only when one attains such a mind will human desires be utterly purified, resulting in perfect penetration and non-obstruction.
If the mind has a dwelling place—if the mind has even a single point of attachment toward the six sense objects—it falls into the trap of others and cannot be free or unencumbered;

this is precisely what constitutes "non-dwelling. Thus, that which is dwelt upon is not the dwelling place of a Bodhisattva. For this reason, the Buddha said that because the mind has something [to which it clings]...
To abide is itself non-abiding;
therefore, the Buddha spoke of the bodhisattva-mind. The Buddha himself said: "When I speak of the bodhisattva-mind, it is fundamentally empty yet luminous.
If one abides in form while engaging in activity, this mind is not awakening. For this reason, the Buddha was resolute [in his teaching].
He speaks of the bodhisattva’s mind:
"One should not abide in form when practicing giving. This is why one does not abide in form when practicing giving.
Subhūti—Subhūti, the Buddha calls out to Subhūti.
Because Bodhisattvas seek to benefit all sentient beings, they give rise to great compassion (mahākaruṇā) on account of those beings.

This is precisely the absence of marks; therefore, it is "non-mark.

They are not sentient beings. If one can turn the light back upon oneself, the deluded mind will naturally depart;
thus, no sentient being can be found, and for this reason, they are not sentient beings.
Subhūti, the Buddha feared that if people were to hear the words of this sutra, they would immediately give rise to alarm, terror, and dread, and thus fail to achieve accomplishment.

The Tathāgata is a speaker of truth. All the dharmas of the prajñāpāramitā spoken by me, the Tathāgata, are unsurpassed bodhi;
they bring about the realization of the fundamental nature. The Tathāgata speaks words that are true and not false.
"Truthful speech" refers to words that are substantial and not hollow.

"Non-deceptive speech" refers to that which is spoken with ultimate sincerity; it is not speech of fraud or delusion.

being shrouded in obscurity and seeing nothing at all, how could the deluded mind ever be brought to subside? Only through awakening...
How can the mind find rest and abide?
Whether it be the bodhisattva’s mind or within the bodhisattva’s mind, once one knows that dharmas should not be dwelt upon, one practices giving without dwelling on dharmas;
thus, one practices giving externally without dwelling on dharmas. This is...
Vajra-eye! Thus, by kindling the lamp of prajñā, one perfectly awakens to the Tathāgata’s unimpeded penetration;
this is the self-manifestation of the unsurpassed true nature.

The light of the sun shines upon them; they further obtain the illumination of the sun's light and behold various forms.
Beholding these various forms, they thoroughly understand all illusory objects and are not bound by them.

The Buddha deeply perceived that the formless dharma of prajñā is truly sufficient to inspire the wholesome minds of people and to restrain their evil intentions.
Subhūti, therefore I call to Subhūti:
in a future age, during the five-hundred-year period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
if there should be sons of good family or daughters of good family who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra— should there be such as these...
If sons or daughters of good family can respectfully receive and uphold this in their hearts, read and recite it, and contemplate its meaning, they will not be disturbed by external objects.
They will naturally abandon evil and practice goodness, practicing giving while detached from signs, and practicing patience while detached from signs.
Although the physical form of the Tathāgata has already entered nirvāṇa, the dharmatā of the Tathāgata remains.
Ever-present and never obscured, penetratingly discerning without omission,
one is immediately the Tathāgata through the Buddha’s wisdom; having reached the stage of Bodhi-awakening,
one becomes the Self-nature Tathāgata-Buddha, possessing the eye of pure wisdom.
The Tathāgata fully knows these people who abandon evil and practice goodness;
he fully sees these people who give alms without dwelling on signs and who practice patience without dwelling on signs.
Out of his original great compassion and his heart to rescue and deliver sentient beings, the Tathāgata especially protects and assists these virtuous people, silently shielding them from behind.
I pray that this person may have all their aspirations fulfilled and attain the accomplishment of immeasurable and boundless merit.

May this person fully accomplish the merit of perceiving the nature of reality (dharmatā), which pervades the entire dharma-realm without limit and remains eternally throughout ten thousand kalpas. How could it be otherwise?
How limited and finite it would be!
Chapter Fifteen: On the Merit of Upholding the Sūtra. Because the merit of receiving and upholding this sūtra is immeasurable, it is called "The Section on the Merit of Upholding the Sūtra."
Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:

"When I was King Kali in the past and my body was being dismembered, I did no more than cite the realms experienced in the past to demonstrate that there are no four marks—self, person, sentient being, or life-spanner—and only then could I practice patience without anger and attain the purity of self-nature. This was not a teaching."
People sacrifice their bodies in their quest for Buddhahood. Furthermore, throughout many kalpas, the Buddha has always been free from these four marks;
only then was he able to enter [this state]. He cuts where there is nothing to cut and severs where there is nothing to sever.

Even though his body is dismembered limb by limb, because he harbors no thought of anger, his body returns to its former state. Were it not for one who has already reached the realm of the Buddha, who could act in such a way?
The Buddha feared that if people were to hear this teaching on the dismemberment of the body, they might instead give rise to doubts and a lack of faith,
leading them to dwell in fear and thoughts of retreat or regret. Furthermore, he feared that those who are stubbornly deluded might cling to the doctrine of giving up the body,
merely offering their own lives as alms, while remaining ignorant of their own mind-nature and the mind-nature of others.
It is of no benefit whatsoever. Therefore, I call upon Subhūti: you shall understand this by comparing it to one who would give their own body as a gift.
Suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, during the first part of the day... [Suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family.]
Within a single day, from dawn until the hour of the Dragon (辰), it constitutes the first portion of the day;

giving away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges during this time constitutes the middle portion of the day. From the hour of the Dragon until the hour of the Sheep (未), it constitutes the middle portion of the day.

until the end of the day, this constitutes the latter part of the day, and one should likewise offer bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Do not say that a single person can offer only a single body—how could such a thing be possible?
If one were to give as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River three times each day;
even if one possessed countless bodies and gave three times every day.

Thus, if one were to give away one's body as an offering for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, reaching even unto incalculable kalpas, the resulting immeasurable merit and retribution would be beyond words.
Nevertheless, such a person could only receive the stubborn, worldly blessings of the mundane realm.
Furthermore, if there is another person who hears this sutra— should anyone hear this Prajñāpāramitā sutra of signlessness—
and with faith does not oppose it, their merit surpasses that [of the former]. They believe that their own mind is originally pure and do not cling to the four [extremes].
This is because [the latter] turns its back on the original aspiration. Its merit surpasses that of one who gives their body as a gift; it is both greater and more enduring.
For although giving one's body may be frequent and long-lasting, it is still a "giving with signs" (*nimitta-dāna*) performed out of a desire to attain Buddhahood.
If, however, one possesses the signless Dharma (*animitta-dharma*) of the sutras and one’s faith is pure, one does not cling to the four [signs].
If one turns one's back on and opposes these signs, then the mind perceives the luminosity of its own nature; all things thus converge.

Is this not superior to the merit of those who give away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet cling to signs and remain deluded in their minds? To hear and believe this without opposition—this is truly supreme.
It would still surpass the merit of giving away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
how much more so to transcribe it, and how much more so to personally transcribe its chapters and verses while investigating and translating their words.
