One does not grasp it through forms and characteristics, nor does one seek it through words and speech. Not only is there no manifold dharma to be attained, but there is not even...
There is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended;
this is what is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is merely a forced designation, called "Anuttara-bodhi" for want of another term.
Essentially, when not a single thought arises and delusion is exhausted so that principle is harmonized, this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As for those who aspire to and cultivate the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how could they be bound by dharmas?
Could it be that they do not realize that the wondrous nature is fundamentally empty and devoid of the characteristics of dharmas?

Chapter Twenty-Three: The Section on Cultivating Goodness with a Pure Mind. Because one cultivates wholesome dharmas with a pure mind, free from the four marks [of self, person, being, and life], and because of this practice of goodness, it is called "The Section on Cultivating Goodness with a Pure Mind."
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying:
"The Dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that I have taught is my own original nature."
This Dharma is equal; it is the bodhi of intrinsic nature. This Dharma does not diminish in ordinary beings nor increase in sages, and thus it is equal.
There is no high or low; while the physical body has high and low, the true nature has neither high nor low.
This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is for this reason that it is named "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Enlightenment. Why is this so?
Because there is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span. This is because the true nature of reality is fundamentally devoid of a self.
These are the delusions of persons, sentient beings, life, and self. If such delusions exist, then sensual desires will be deep and the celestial faculties (tianji) will necessarily be shallow;
the burden of grasping and seizing will remain, and the profound unity will not be complete. I see that various differences arise amidst the mundane dusts;
how could these be the Dharma of equality? Only when the Dharma is equal can it be called unsurpassed bodhi.
One should cultivate all wholesome dharmas. The Buddha further taught that one must cultivate these all wholesome dharmas.
Whether it be giving, observing the precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom—all of these are wholesome dharmas for clarifying the mind and perceiving its nature.
By practicing according to these dharmas, one empties the self to illuminate the truth, honors virtue and treads the Way, and ultimately reaches the stage of supreme enlightenment.
One immediately attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; that is, one immediately attains this anuttara-bodhi.
However, there is also the fear that people might become mired in the notion of existent dharmas.
Subhūti, therefore I address Subhūti:
that which is called "wholesome dharmas," that which is called "wholesome dharmas," is the gateway for guiding and leading sentient beings toward the human realm.
Originally, these wholesome dharmas do not exist; they are merely provisional names used to awaken people.
If one practices without dwelling in the four marks, then practice is identical to non-practice.
The Tathāgata says that even wholesome dharmas are not wholesome dharmas. If one clings to wholesome dharmas, then there will be the marks of a person, a self, and so forth.
These are called wholesome dharmas; these are called wholesome dharmas. To practice without abiding in the four marks is to practice that which is without anything practiced.
Such practice becomes the cause for attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is thus.
This is called true cultivation. It is attained by not dwelling in any phenomena; it is the attainment of non-attainment.
To directly attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is what is called true attainment. This is precisely the meaning of my statement that there is not the slightest dharma to be attained.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The Incomparable Merit of Wisdom. Giving constitutes merit; upholding this sutra constitutes wisdom.
When merit is compared with wisdom, merit does not equal wisdom; therefore, it is called the Incomparable Merit of Wisdom.

Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "I have taught that by practicing all wholesome dharmas while remaining free from the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is truly because, by practicing wholesome dharmas while detached from these four marks, one realizes liberation from the four evil karmas of greed, anger, ignorance, and attachment."
The six sense objects cannot defile one another; likewise, the six perfections are without abiding, all mental conceptions are completely forgotten, and consciousness is entirely extinguished.
This profoundly serene and pure mind truly transcends into the realm of the Great Void, whereby one attains unsurpassed Bodhi.
I contemplate the method of practicing goodness through formlessness, and the true realization attained is such as this unsurpassed Bodhi.
By means of the pure and unconditioned Way, their minds transcend the triple world and exist eternally through kalpas;
how could their merit and virtue possibly have an equal?
If all the Sumeru Kings and all the various [mountains] within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system...
Mount Sumeru, King of Mountains, reaching upward to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and downward to the limits of Mount Kunlun—such heaps of the seven treasures;
even if one were to take heaps of these seven treasures as vast and high as Mount Sumeru.
If someone takes this and uses it for giving, that gift may be called great.
Because of such a cause of great giving, one will certainly obtain such a fruit; the merit thus acquired should also be great and inexhaustible.
If a person takes this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
or if a person takes even as much as a four-line verse from the Prajñā Sūtra, including that four-line verse.
To receive, uphold, read, and recite [this teaching]; to receive and uphold it so that it enters the mind;
to explain it for others and to expound it for others—this brings benefit to the world.
Compared to the previous merit of giving the seven treasures, [the merit of this practice] far surpasses it.
A hundredth part does not equal it; a hundredth part does not equal even one part of the merit of upholding this sutra.
Even a hundred-thousand-millionth part—even a hundred-thousand-millionth part—and indeed any calculation or analogy cannot reach it; none can equal the merit of upholding this sutra.
One part of this is that people can practice giving by seeking only outwardly, without seeking within the mind.

Yet, by upholding, reciting, and explaining even a single four-line verse for others—thereby benefiting both self and others—one directly enables oneself and others to realize together the Great Way of Unsurpassed Bodhi.
This leads to this very Prajñā, which is suchness itself, immovable and unchanging.

His light pervades everywhere without exception; his transformations reach all places without fail. Even heaven and earth cannot encompass or support him; even the fires at the end of an eon cannot destroy him.

He permeates all things without leaving anything out, and both devas and humans rely upon him. When viewing the height of Mount Sumeru, it is not even comparable to a single mote of dust within a trichiliocosm.
How could the merit of such generosity ever compare to that of one who upholds this sutra?
It is through comparative deliberation that one reaches a judgment.
○ Section Twenty-Five: Transformation Without an Object of Transformation. The fundamental nature of all sentient beings is inherently good; how could there be anything to be transformed?
Therefore, it is called the section on "Transformation Without an Object of Transformation."
Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "I declare that this Dharma is equal, without high or low.
Because it is devoid of self, person, sentient being, or life-span, by cultivating all wholesome dharmas, one immediately attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is because all sentient beings each possess the nature of true thusness (tathatā) equally."
Thus, there is neither saint nor ordinary person; there is no distinction of high or low. Sentient beings and Buddhas share the same source.
If one can cultivate all wholesome dharmas while remaining free from the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span, then sentient beings are themselves the Tathāgata.
How could there be any sentient beings to be delivered?
"What do you think? What is your thought?
You should not suppose that the Tathāgata thinks thus; you who study the Way, do not suppose that I, the Tathāgata, truly have such an intention."
"I shall deliver sentient beings. There must indeed be such a mind to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Subhūti, the Buddha called out to Subhūti, saying:
"Do not form this thought. You all must not form this thought that the Tathāgata delivers sentient beings."
Why is this? Why is this? Do not harbor such thoughts. For this Dharma is equal; it has neither high nor low.
Where there is no high, there is no Tathāgata who delivers sentient beings; where there is no low, there are no sentient beings to be delivered.

In truth, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers. Even if there were sentient beings who cling to the four marks, whose natures are deluded and whose minds are confused, the Tathāgata, having no choice, preaches the Dharma to shatter their attachments.
Yet, in awakening them from their delusions, the Tathāgata speaks the Dharma free from marks and delivers beings free from marks;
how could he harbor such a thought as, "I see sentient beings who can be delivered, and I am the one capable of delivering them"?
He delivers them; yet, in his delivering, there is no delivering. Furthermore, there is truly no sentient being whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were sentient beings, or if there were those who hear this sutra and awaken to the Way, these sentient beings would naturally be transformed and delivered.
What need would there be for me to deliver them? This is what is meant by the Buddha of the Equal and True Dharma-realm: he does not deliver sentient beings.

Regarding those "saved by the Tathāgata": if one says that all sentient beings must necessarily be transformed and saved by the Tathāgata, then the Tathāgata would possess the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span;
the Tathāgata would then possess the mark of a self that is capable of saving others.
The mark of the person being saved, the mark of the sentient beings who can be saved, the mark of "I" having already attained Buddhahood,
and the mark of a life-span that remains indestructible for eternal kalpas— if one possesses these four marks, how could one possibly realize the state of a Tathāgata?
Furthermore, how could one possibly save sentient beings?
Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "The Tathāgata truly has no four marks—self, person, sentient being, or life-span—by which he realizes the state of a Tathāgata."
When the Tathāgata speaks of a self, it is merely following conventional usage in accordance with worldly discourse. Although he speaks of a self with his mouth, there is no such self;
just as within the mind there is no such self.
Yet ordinary people cling to appearances and their minds are deluded;
ordinary people do not understand the meaning of being free from appearances, and thus they think, "There is a self," O Subhūti. The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are by nature fundamentally equal and share the same source as the Buddhas; there is no distinction of high or low between them.

Yet, the Tathāgata says they are not truly ordinary beings because, due to their attachment to the four marks—the self (*ātman*), the person (*pudgala*), the sentient being (*sattva*), and the life-span (*jīva*)—they fail to cultivate all wholesome dharmas, thereby causing their true nature to become obscured.
This is called an ordinary person; this is called an ordinary person.

○ Chapter Twenty-Six: The Dharma-body is Without Characteristics. Because the unconditioned Dharma-body is free from conditioned characteristics, it is called "The Dharma-body is Without Characteristics."
Subhūti, the Buddha called out to Subhūti, saying: "When I say that the Tathāgata speaks of 'self,' it is not that there is a self;
yet ordinary people conceive of a self. That which is 'no-self' is the Tathāgata, while that which has a 'self' is an ordinary person.
How can one fail to deeply clarify and thoroughly awaken to the principle of signlessness? [End of previous section]

You have already understood the thirty-two marks. They cannot be seen; that is to say, although the Tathāgata may be perceived through his response-body (nirmāṇakāya) characterized by marks, he cannot be [fully] seen by means of such marks.
What do you think? What is your opinion?
Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? Is it possible to perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks?
Subhūti said: Subhūti’s intention was that the marks and signs of the response body (nirmāṇakāya) must flow forth from within the dharma-body (dharmakāya).

Only when there is something internal does it first manifest externally. If the dharma-body within its nature were not complete, how could it possibly possess these thirty-two kinds of marks and signs?
"It is so, it is so. Therefore, he replied, "It is so, it is so.
To perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks—if one wishes to perceive the Tathāgata, one does not go beyond these thirty-two marks.

The Buddha said, "Subhūti, Subhūti. Having heard Subhūti’s response—that he judges the Tathāgata by means of his marks and signs—the Buddha knew that Subhūti still harbored subtle delusions regarding the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*) and had not yet eliminated them.
Therefore, he raised a mundane matter as a test so that Subhūti’s lack of discernment would become self-evident. For this reason, he addressed Subhūti, saying:
If one were to perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, and if the Tathāgata could indeed be seen through those thirty-two marks,
then the Cakravartin King— this Cakravartin King— who dwells in heaven as one of the Four Great Heavenly Kings and oversees the human realm, [would likewise be perceived thus].
Acting as both a sage and a king, he likewise exhorted and restrained the people regarding good and evil.
Having once cultivated the thirty-two pure practices, he consequently attained the thirty-two marks and secondary characteristics.

However, because he still possessed a mind subject to arising and ceasing, he could not—like the Buddha—be eternally liberated from the cycle of rebirth, remaining unchanging and immutable, without beginning or end, with his transformative influence perpetually enduring.
"Breathing" is itself the Tathāgata. The nature of the Tathāgata’s path is eternally present; it is unconditioned and self-governing.
How could it be within the reach of even a Wheel-Turning Sage King? Subhūti has already realized the Samādhi of Non-contention and attained the foremost path of an Arhat."
Those who cannot attain Buddhahood do so only because this mark of a single hair-tip has not yet been discarded.
Now, having heard the Buddha’s analogy of the wheel-turning sage-king, these slight traces have been swept away entirely into emptiness.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, according to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, and according to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught regarding the Wheel-Turning Sage King..."
"One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One knew that Subhūti had already thoroughly penetrated the dharma of signless true emptiness;
yet he feared that all sentient beings of the present and future might ruin their vision and hearing, failing to awaken to the true nature.
And he spoke in verse. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses. As for "verses" (gāthā), they are sentences formed by the utterance of words.
To see me in form, Or to seek me in sound— Such people follow a deviant path And cannot perceive the Tathāgata.
For the Tathāgata of true nature cannot be seen by looking, nor heard by listening.
How can one perceive by means of form or seek by means of sound? If one perceives by means of form or seeks by means of sound, such a person does not achieve awakening.
To follow one's inherent nature is called the Way; it is like abandoning the correct path and failing to travel upon it, thereby proceeding along a deviant path.
How could such a person be able to see the Tathāgata of true nature? The Buddha, with compassion and equanimity, only wishes that all sentient beings may be liberated from the realms of suffering.
Therefore, one should strictly refrain from outward pursuit and seeking. One should desire that people instead seek within themselves alone.
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to such things as the adornment of Buddha images; "seeing" (*darśana*) means beholding them with one's own eyes.

"Sound" (*śabda*) refers to such things as chanting, praising the *brahman*, and lecturing; "seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*) means searching for them. "I" (*ātman*) is the Buddha’s own designation. "Heterodox paths" (*mithyāmārga*) refers to...
Because sounds and forms are merely illusory and false, only the true nature (*dharmatā*) constitutes perfect awakening (*samyaksambodhi*).
The Tathāgata is the Buddha of the Dharma-body of the true nature.
○ Chapter Twenty-seven: No Cessation and No Extinction. Because phenomena have neither cessation nor extinction, it is called "no cessation and no extinction."
The Section on Cessation.

Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "Since you already know that one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, and that the Tathāgata cannot be seen through form nor sought through sound, you have realized the dharma of signlessness."
Deeply understand this: at such a time, there is not a single thing in your mind; it is completely swept away into total emptiness.
Yet, at this moment, you must not cling to this non-existence, lest you fall into the extreme of nihilism. For clinging to existence and clinging to non-existence are both outside the Way.
If you should have such a thought, if you should harbor this notion:
that the Tathāgata does not [attain Buddhahood] by means of the marks of perfection, nor does he rely upon the marks of perfection.
"One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having attained this unsurpassed enlightenment, Subhūti—Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:
'Do not conceive such a thought. You must by no means speak with such a notion.'"
The Tathāgata does not exist by virtue of possessing marks of perfection. Originally, there is no sound or form of the Tathāgata to be sought;
he is not defined by the thirty-two marks, nor does he depend upon the merit of perfected, pure, and wondrous conduct.
One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. One suddenly attains this Great Path of Bodhi.
Subhūti, the Buddha called out to Subhūti, saying:
If you should have such a thought, and I were to admonish you not to have it, it would be for the sake of setting you up as a model for the assembly and a mirror for future students.
If you were to be attached [to the idea that] one does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the marks of perfection (*lakṣaṇa*), you would form such a notion.
Those who resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* speak of the annihilation and cessation of all phenomena (*dharma*).
As I understand it, there is truly no such phenomenon as one who resolves their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is because, according to the meaning of the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena, they are neither real nor unreal; it does not mean that all phenomena are annihilated or ceased.
Do not harbor such thoughts. If you were to entertain this notion, it would be a great error, for it implies the total annihilation of all phenomena.
Why is this? For what reason do I say so?
Those who resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*— those who give rise to the bodhicitta—
must necessarily rely upon the Dharma of Prajñā as the instrument for their practice. If this Dharma were not employed, by what means could the flower of the mind blossom?
Regarding the Dharma, I do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation; therefore, I do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation here.
Section Twenty-Eight: Non-Appropriation and Non-Attachment. Regarding the merit performed by a bodhisattva, there is no thought of self-appropriation and no notion of greedy attachment;
hence it is called the Section on Non-Appropriation and Non-Attachment.
Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "When I say that the Tathāgata speaks of a 'self,' it is not that there is a self.
One should not regard the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. Do not harbor such a thought;
the Tathāgata does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi because he possesses these marks. It is truly because there is no mark of a self."
Thus, there is no attachment to a self; all dharmas are entirely without self. Since the characteristic of self is absent, all characteristics are empty.
The pure mind is as tranquil and vast as great space; therefore, regarding the thirty-two marks, one does not dwell in existence.
Endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, they do not abide in non-existence; they exist yet do not exist, and are non-existent yet do not cease to exist.

In accordance with causes and conditions, they remain without the slightest stirring of thought. By accomplishing the mind of emptiness and quiescence through the patience of emptiness (*śūnyatākṣānti*), they truly realize the unsurpassed, unconditioned Great Way.
If a bodhisattva were to offer the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,

yet that bodhisattva who has resolved upon the great mind of unsurpassed enlightenment does not realize the dharma of non-self, it would be in vain for them to possess those seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
To practice giving while maintaining such [self-centered] thoughts is to possess a self-conception that craves merit;
this is utterly incompatible with the Great Way’s ultimate impartiality and selflessness. How, then, could it possibly fill heaven and earth and transform and nurture all living beings?
Furthermore, if there is a person who knows that all phenomena are without self;

or if there is a person who deeply understands that all myriad dharmas arise from one's own mind, which is as tranquil as the great void, neither abiding nor clinging, and in which no sense of "self" exists.
"I" refers to the mind of self-centeredness. "Accomplished" means to achieve perfection.
"To have accomplished patience" means to have achieved this merit of forbearance.
"This bodhisattva" refers to these aforementioned bodhisattvas.
This surpasses the previous bodhisattvas; it surpasses the bodhisattva who gave the gift of jewels.
The merit obtained, the merit thus acquired—why is this? Why is this so?
Subhūti, fearing that Subhūti might mistakenly regard worldly merit as true merit, the Buddha called out to him again and said:
"Because all bodhisattvas possess the mind of non-apprehension."

It is because they do not accept merit; it is because they do not accept merit that they are superior. Subhūti, based on the appearance of not accepting merit, suspects that the fruit follows from the cause.
If one were to stubbornly adhere to non-acceptance, there would necessarily be the mark of a fixed self;
how could such a person be considered superior?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Subhūti has not yet understood its meaning.
World-Honored One, I ask the World-Honored One:
why does a bodhisattva not accept merit? Why does a bodhisattva not accept merit?"
Subhūti. The Buddha called to Subhūti and revealed to him the Dharma of the mind:
"The merit performed by a bodhisattva is not held with a mind of self-reception. With single-mindedness, they know only this:
'I desire to bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa. They simply wish that all sentient beings may fully receive this merit. Once all sentient beings have been brought to parinirvāṇa..."
One does not conceive of oneself as the one who can deliver others, nor does one know that there are actually sentient beings whom one delivers.
One should not harbor attachment; it is through such a mind free from attachment that the fruit of true awakening (bodhi) is realized.
Therefore, it is said that one does not accept merit. This is why it is said that a bodhisattva does not accept merit.

○ Section Twenty-nine: Tranquility of Dignified Conduct (*Iryāpatha*). Regarding the four dignified conducts of coming, going, sitting, and lying down: when coming and going are in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*), they constitute tranquility;
hence it is called the "Section on the Tranquility of Dignified Conduct."
Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "I declare that all dharmas are without self; thus one attains the realization of patience (*kṣānti*).
This is to be free from all marks (*nimitta*) and thereby perceive the Tathāgata as the true nature (*dharmatā*)."

If someone were to say: "Suppose there is someone who, failing to realize this principle, says that the Tathāgata possesses a body adorned with the marks and signs, and that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down; that he comes or goes, sits or lies down..."
To benefit all sentient beings—such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught. Such a person does not understand that all dharmas I have taught are without self;
they have attained the mind of patience (*kṣānti*).
Why is this? Why do you not understand the intent of what I have said?

It is because people are attached to the physical marks and features of the Tathāgata’s response-body (nirmāṇakāya), [believing] that he truly comes and goes. You must know that the true nature of each person is fully complete within themselves.
Originally unborn and undying, the Way’s transformation is eternally present. If one truly knows that all dharmas are without self, one attains patience (*kṣānti*).
Unobscured by the six sense-objects and unconfined by the marks of phenomena, the true nature of suchness remains unmoving;
though it is signless and unconditioned, it naturally encompasses all dharmas, its light pervading everywhere without exception.
His transformations reach everywhere without exception; he transcends the three realms and abides eternally throughout kalpas.
As for "Tathāgata," as for "Tathāgata," it refers to that which accords with its own intrinsic nature.
He has come from nowhere; he comes as such.
He has come from nowhere, nor does he go anywhere; he neither goes nor departs.
Therefore he is called the Tathāgata. Therefore he is called the Tathāgata. He resolves his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One should know that all phenomena are without self; this constitutes the meaning of attaining *kṣānti* (patience).

Since one has long since departed from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the Tathāgata, whose true nature is pure, naturally does not give rise to a mind that clings to the coming, going, sitting, or reclining of a Tathāgata.
Master Changshui said: "It is like the moon appearing when the water is clear; it is not [that the moon moves into the water]."

When the moon comes, the water becomes turbid and the moon appears hidden; yet it is not that the moon has departed. It is because of the clarity or turbidity of the water that [the moon's appearance changes], not because the moon itself rises or sinks.
When the mind is pure, one sees the Buddha; this is not because the Buddha has come. When the mind is defiled, one does not see him; this is not because the Buddha has gone.
Since the human mind possesses both defilement and purity, the Buddha fundamentally has neither coming nor going.
Section Thirty-one: The Integration of Principle and Phenomena (Yihe Lixiang Fen). This integrates with the true nature; this constitutes the characteristic of the principle of nature.
Therefore, it is called "The Section on the Integration of Principle and Phenomena.
Subhūti—The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "I say that if there were someone who claimed that the Tathāgata comes or goes..."
Whether walking, sitting, or lying down, such a person clings to the arising of signs and gives rise to thoughts;
they do not understand the meaning of my teaching that all phenomena are without self. With such attachment, amidst the mundane world, all objects are delusive.
Those who stir their thoughts upon contact are as numerous as the atoms of dust resulting from that crushing; they are beyond measure.
If a son or daughter of good family were to crush this great trichiliocosm into minute particles, reducing it to such fine motes of dust—
"What do you think? What is your opinion?
Would that multitude of atoms be considered many?
"It would be very many," Subhūti replied. Subhūti, having deeply realized the Buddha’s intention, said, "Very many."
“World-Honored One,” he addressed the World-Honored One to inquire and seek clarification:
“For what reason? For what reason is it said to be so very much? It is because all afflictions (*kleśa*) are dispersed throughout the sensory realms;
those who stir their thoughts upon encountering objects are beyond counting, and thus are said to be very many. Yet, although these fine motes of dust are numerous, they are nonetheless empty.”
The substance of delusion is a non-solid essence; it arises as soon as thought moves and ceases as soon as thought is stilled.
It is fundamentally not solid or real, yet it appears to exist constantly.
If these multitudes of atoms were truly existent, then these multitudes of atoms would all be merely the false imaginings of the human mind.

[Śāriputra] stood up. [The Buddha said: "If it were truly the case that there were as many of these atoms as you say, the Buddha would not call them a 'multitude of atoms. The Buddha would simply not say they are a 'multitude of atoms.'"
Why is this so? Because delusive objects are all external things; they do not inherently exist within our own nature.
If one can keep the mirror of the mind ever clear, then even though fine dust may be abundant, it cannot come into contact with it. How, then, could it obscure my spiritual treasury?
The Buddha said that the multitude of subtle particles is not, in fact, a multitude of subtle particles.

That which is not a multitude of subtle particles is called a "multitude of subtle particles. If one cannot awaken to the true mind and remains deluded by all sensory objects (dust), this is called a "multitude of subtle particles.
Since the world is composed of the accumulation of subtle particles, if there are no subtle particles, how can there be a world?
The worlds of atoms are all merely provisional designations of form and appearance; fundamentally, they are not real.

Within the great void, atoms drift like wandering vapors, arising and ceasing at will. Within the great void, worlds consist of light and darkness, color and emptiness, mountains, rivers, and the great earth, gathering and dispersing as they please.
If it were the true nature of *prajñā*, it would remain indestructible throughout kalpas; how could it be otherwise?
"How comparable this is!
World-Honored One, Subhūti has attained profound realization. He then addressed the World-Honored One once more:
"The Tathāgata has taught that the trichiliocosm is entirely formed by the accumulation of delusory objects. [As for] kalpas..."
When their number is exhausted, they ultimately undergo transformation and decay. This is why they are empty, false, and unreal;
they are not truly worlds. They are merely called "worlds" because they still exist for the present moment.
This is what is meant by "world. This is what is meant by "world."
Why is this? Subhūti further questions and explains: Why is it called "not a world"?

It is because a world is formed by the accumulation of atoms, and a world can be analyzed into minute atoms; thus, worlds all belong to the realm of the illusory and will ultimately meet with destruction.
It is not that there exists, from the outset, a substantial nature that is indestructible. Therefore, the commentary states:
"If the world were truly existent—if one were to regard the world as truly existent—it would necessarily be the primordial true nature.
From beginningless time, it has been eternally abiding and imperishable. Because this truly real nature exists within the world..."
Within the realm, all is forged into a single whole. There is nothing that lingers in the traces of phenomena, yet nothing that sinks into emptiness.
This is precisely the "single integrated mark" (*ekaghanalakṣaṇa*). It is one, yet it cannot be joined to make two;
it is joined, yet it cannot be split to make separate parts. This is the true nature of the single integrated mark.

The Tathāgata speaks of a "single unified mark," yet the true nature of this single unified mark spoken of by the Tathāgata is such that it has no form that can be seen and no sound that can be heard.
The Tathāgata, having departed from marks, speaks of a single unified mark;
it must not be grasped as being substantially existent.
It is not a unified whole (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, it cannot be grasped as being truly non-existent;
this is what is called a "unified whole," for it is merely given the forced name "unified whole.
Subhūti, the Buddha, seeing that Subhūti’s words had already led him to enter into and deeply understand [the truth], called out to him once more.
He said:

"The 'unified totality' (yī hé xiàng) is the essence of true nature, empty and spiritual. That it possesses neither form nor color, nor sound, means that one should only engage in self-examination and self-awakening;
having [phenomena], yet not being obstructed by their traces; being without [substantiality], yet not sinking into emptiness. This is true emptiness."
It is not empty; it is wondrously beyond words.
This is precisely what is unspeakable.

Those who seek it through speech and description are merely ordinary people, mere commoners, who do not understand that encountering characteristics is to be separated from characteristics, and encountering emptiness is to be separated from [emptiness].
Regarding the meaning of emptiness:
they are greedily attached to its phenomena; they are greedily attached to the objective appearances of sensory realms.

They take the world of subtle atoms to be truly existent and take the physical body and the six sense faculties to be the true self. Because they do not awaken to the true nature of numinous clarity, they sink into the cycle of rebirth.
There is no means by which one may attain liberation.
○ Chapter Thirty-one: The Non-arising of Knowledge and Vision. When knowledge and vision are free from seeing, this is right view.
When non-arising is itself non-birth, this is constant birth. Therefore, it is called "The Section on the Non-arising of Knowledge and Vision."
Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:

"In the Prajñā Sūtras, the reason why the four-line verse on non-characteristics (*animitta*) is repeatedly debated and progressively compared for its superiority is that, regarding the meaning of these four lines, those with shallow faith may thereby shatter their attachments and awaken from delusion, while those with deep faith and understanding may thereby abide in the truth and subdue the false. To the end...
Reaching the ultimate limit, one simply causes the wisdom of *prajñā* to fill the heavens and earth and transcend the three realms.
Without moving a single step, in the mere snap of a finger, one arrives at the shore of the *pāramitās*. For this reason, I do not avoid the reproach of being prolix;
I am eager to cause others to believe and understand. However, appearances arise from views; such is the view of having appearances.
These would then constitute false views. Only the view of signlessness is the true view; yet even this cannot be attained.

Therefore, one must employ these four views to mutually clarify and distinguish them, so that those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta may gain faith and understanding, abandon delusion, and return to the truth.
Yet we have equally realized the unsurpassed, unconditioned Great Way; this is my profound intention.
The Buddha feared that people might become attached to false views and thus be unable to see their true nature, and so he posed this question.
If someone were to say that the Buddha taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span;
or if someone were to say that the Buddha taught these four views of self,
person, and so forth— Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:
What do you think? What is your opinion?
Does this person understand the meaning of what I have said? Does this person understand the meaning of what I have taught regarding true vision and false vision?
"No, World-Honored One. Subhūti answered "No" to the Buddha.
He then addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken. Although the meaning of the four views is simple, its principle is in fact profound."
Subtle! To cling to existence or to cling to non-existence—neither is the true vision. Unless one is profoundly awakened, none can fathom its profundity.
If all people fail to understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught, [they remain deluded].
For what reason? Subhūti further inquires and explains why: "World-Honored One, those people do not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken.
Thus he addresses the World-Honored One.
It is said that there are views of self, views of persons, views of sentient beings, and views of life-spanners.

Indeed, when the Tathāgata speaks of views of self, views of persons, views of sentient beings, and views of life-spanners, he means that the nature of these views is without seeking and without attainment; they are profoundly still and eternally abiding.
Thus, by means of the pure view of self, one perceives the true nature of persons as each being fully complete within themselves; this is the pure view of persons.
Furthermore, within the true nature (*dharmatā*), there are fundamentally no afflictions (*kleśa*) to be severed; this is because sentient beings perceive it with purity.
One perceives that self-nature (*svabhāva*) is unchanging and undifferentiated, without arising or ceasing; this is because one perceives it with purity as a "life-principle" (*jīva*).
These four views are what the Buddha taught; they are the true perception of self-nature. If sentient beings, regarding these, do not harbor attachment...
In the midst of grasping and rejecting, they cling to views at every turn; encountering form, they receive it, and meeting an object, they contact it.
Clinging to all forms and appearances, they fall into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Such individuals are truly unable to believe in or understand the meaning of the four views.
Even those who have deep faith yet lack deep understanding, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*), will consequently cling to the four [views].
To take characteristics as being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) yet fail to achieve their harmonious integration and vital activity leads one to fall into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
This is like withered wood or extinguished ashes, lacking the potential for sprouting and growth; it likewise prevents the essence of *prajñā* from becoming perfectly pervasive and all-encompassing.
Such a state is also incapable of believing in or understanding the meaning of the four views.
This is not the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span. Clinging to existence and clinging to non-existence are both deluded views;
this is the true view regarding the absence of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.
This is called the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span. It is simply not clinging to existence, nor clinging to non-existence;
it is existence that is not existence, and non-existence that is not non-existence. One does not fall into the view of eternalism, nor does one fall into the view of annihilationism.

Having spontaneously realized the perfect integration of the *dharmatā*, one remains profoundly still and eternally pure. This is called the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.
This is what I have taught. They have not yet awakened to or deeply understood it; such people simply do not comprehend the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken.
Subhūti, when the Buddha heard Subhūti’s explanation of the meaning of these four views, he was profoundly enlightened and thoroughly penetrated it. He understood it completely.
Having attained the state of no-remainder, he truly conformed to the Buddha’s intention. He then called out to Bodhi, saying:
"Those who resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and who are able to give rise to the true mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—"
Regarding all phenomena, one should know them thus; one should realize them thus so as not to fall into the view of eternalism or the view of nihilism.
Regarding such views, one should give rise to them thus so as not to fall into the view of eternalism or the view of nihilism.
One should have such faith and understanding; one should thus give rise to a faith and understanding that does not fall into eternalism or nihilism.
One should not give rise to the conceptual mark of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), nor give rise to the conceptual mark of the dharma of faith and understanding regarding knowledge and vision.

Although the Buddha demonstrates through the non-arising of the conceptual mark of dharmas, it is still difficult for those who practice, cultivate, and realize to attain the non-arising of the conceptual mark of dharmas.
Subhūti, the Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying:
"As for what is called the 'characteristic of dharmas,' within the Tathāgata’s mind there is no perception of the characteristic of dharmas; it merely accords with external manifestations."
There is neither reality nor emptiness.

The Tathāgata says that these are not dharmic characteristics; rather, he provisionally employs them to untangle people's attachments and release their fetters, enabling them to give rise to the true and subdue the delusive.
This is called the characteristic of dharmas; it is merely a provisional designation for the characteristic of dharmas.

Since the characteristic of dharmas is not necessarily devoid of views regarding self, person, sentient being, or life-span, it is that which the true mind of bodhi should know and see, and that which one should believe and understand.
How can those who have resolved to attain bodhi fail to examine this? To know thus and to see thus is precisely [the state where] there is none.
This is the true knowledge and true vision of supreme enlightenment. "Dharma" refers to phenomena; "characteristics" refers to outward traces.
As for the characteristics of arising phenomena, regarding the traces of phenomena, views such as those of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span do not at all sprout within the mind.

Chapter Thirty-Two: The Section on the Non-Reality of Manifestations. Dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew, and lightning—all these are the provisional manifestations of impermanent transformations;
they are not the true, real, and eternally abiding essence. Therefore, this is called the section on the non-reality of manifestations.

Subhūti, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "As you have understood it, to see that within the true nature there are fundamentally no four marks—self, person, sentient being, or life-span—is precisely the true vision of the pure self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
I say that according to the meaning of what you have understood, one should know, see, and believe in this way."
Understanding that the characteristics of dharmas regarding knowledge, vision, faith, and resolution do not arise, then all conditions are entirely empty and all dharmas return to the source.

Thus, one’s deportment is tranquil and still, and knowledge and vision do not arise. One’s nature accords with the path of unsurpassed Bodhi, and the mind is the true reality of *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
This causes the profoundly serene and pure mind to pervade the three realms throughout kalpas.
It exists eternally. There is nothing that is not born. The production of things is unfathomable.
Suppose there were someone who offered as many jewels of the seven treasures as would fill immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds;

or suppose there were someone who offered as many jewels of the seven treasures as would fill immeasurable and infinite worlds—where "immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds" does not merely stop at a limit.
If one were to take [these] as many as the sands of the Ganges and use them for giving, bestowing them as alms upon others, this would certainly constitute worldly merit. However,
if there is a son or daughter of good family who gives rise to the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva, awakening the mind of universal salvation toward Bodhi...
As for the mind:
it upholds this sutra, upholds the verses of this sutra,
even as few as four lines of verse, and even perceives the four lines of verse on signlessness within one's own nature.
By upholding, reciting, and chanting it, one personally realizes one's own nature;
by expounding it for others, and further propagating and explaining it to instruct people, they too shall attain clarity of mind and realization of their true nature.
That merit is superior to the former; it is indeed supramundane merit. It accomplishes both oneself and others, and the enjoyment of its blessings is inexhaustible.
How could it not surpass the merit of one who takes the seven treasures filling immeasurable and incalculable worlds and uses them for giving?
How does one expound the Dharma for others without grasping at appearances, remaining as-it-is (tathatā) and unmoving? Why is this?
The Buddha further questioned himself, saying: "As for what I call 'not grasping at appearances' and 'remaining as-it-is and unmoving,' why is this so?
It is because the true nature is profoundly still and eternally quiescent; it is without appearance and without conditioned activity, being inherently as-it-is from the very beginning.
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there is not a single noble one or sage who has not realized enlightenment (*bodhi*) through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If all worldly conditioned phenomena were entirely false and unreal, [how could this be so?]

It is like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; like the unreality of a false dream, like the artificial transformations of a magical illusion, like the arising and ceasing of water bubbles, like the flickering of a shadow’s form, and like a dream that emerges from a mindless state yet appears as if possessing intention.
Awakening from a dream is entering into illusion; the formation of illusion is the binding of doubtful dreams;
both arise from inversion. They are like dew and like lightning: like morning dew that easily dries, like a flash of lightning that quickly fades.
A bubble forms upon water and vanishes with the water; a shadow is cast by a form and perishes as the form ceases. All are taking the void for reality.
Dew is dried by the sun; lightning disperses with the clearing of the sky. These are especially fleeting in their arising and ceasing.
One should contemplate them in this way; one should practice these six contemplations. As for the contemplation of the six: they are characterized by arising and ceasing, and are impermanent.
Since they are empty, false, and unsubstantial, one knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) possess form and appearance, and are thus deceptive and unreal.
Only my true nature—suchness (*tathatā*)—is immovable; it is without form and without appearance.
It does not decay even after arising through ten thousand kalpas; it neither arises nor ceases, remaining eternally present throughout antiquity. It is able, within the formless...
As for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this verse to others—how could their merit possibly be measured or conceived?
Within these six characters, the responses of human affairs, the stability of mountains and rivers, and the transformations of heaven and earth are all fully expounded.
These four lines exhaust the essential meaning of the scriptures; they are truly the Tathāgata’s own [teaching].

It is the place where all things are extinguished; one contemplates that nothing is possessed. This is the wondrous wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama*).
After the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra—having repeatedly elucidated the Dharma of Prajñā—he concluded his discourse.

The Elder Subhūti, who had first initiated the request; the Elder Subhūti, who had suddenly awakened to true emptiness and already heard the seal of the mind—those present in the assembly listening to the Dharma at that time.
As for the bhikṣus: there are those who are bhikṣus and yet are called "Seng" (Saṃgha).
As for the bhikṣuṇīs: there are those who are bhikṣuṇīs and yet are called "Shigou" (Upādhyāyī).
As for the upāsakas: there are laymen who are referred to as upāsakas.
Upāsikā. There are female practitioners who are called upāsikās.
All those in the world—devas, humans, and asuras; all the gods who protect the Dharma in the heavens and among humans, including the asuras.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken—having heard this sutra spoken by the Buddha—they were all filled with great joy.
Each beheld their own nature without alarm, without terror, and without fear;
they were all filled with great joy, fortunate that the True Dharma is so difficult to encounter, and delighted to have personally met it this day.
Believe, accept, and practice [this]. May there be none who do not believe and accept these words, but instead take them to heart, practice these teachings, and propagate them to others.
Though one passes through billions of kalpas, one will eternally realize the indestructible diamond body.
The Buddha’s grace and compassion are ultimate. Those who contemplate this sutra—how could they fail to proclaim the wondrous Dharma as a way to repay the Buddha’s grace?
Master Chuanshan’s verse says: Hungry, one finds food; thirsty, one finds drink. The sick find recovery; those oppressed by heat find coolness.
A poor man encounters treasure; an infant sees its mother. A drifting boat reaches the shore; a solitary traveler returns home. In drought, one meets sweet rain;
the land possesses loyal and virtuous men. The four barbarian tribes fold their hands; the eight quarters submit. Every point is thus; every thing fully manifests.
Throughout all ages, from the ordinary to the sagely; across the hells and heavens, the east, west, south, and north—there is no need for deliberation.
All beings within lands as numerous as the atoms and sands of the universe enter entirely into the Great Vajra Dharma-Assembly.
